title: Atomic movies of elementary chemical steps without a photo-trigger

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a reliable way to reconstruct the ordered atomic changes of an elementary chemical step initiated by substrate addition, heat, voltage or another non-photochemical trigger. It would produce a time-ordered series of electron-density maps with enough spatial and effective temporal resolution to distinguish the relevant structures and establish their sequence. The measured chemistry would also need to represent the intended reaction, rather than a different pathway imposed by crystallization or experimental conditions. This is a proposed capability whose defining advance is broad access to validated elementary-step sequences.

An atomic movie in this context is a reconstruction from diffraction measurements collected at different reaction delays, often across many crystals. Each map can contain overlapping populations of reactants, intermediates and products. Establishing a chemical sequence therefore requires population analysis, structural refinement and mechanistic interpretation; a succession of maps does not automatically identify a unique pathway. Selected mixing-triggered enzyme measurements already provide part of this capability, so the frontier concerns breadth, temporal resolution and interpretability rather than the first observation of any non-photoactive reaction.

significance.text: If achieved across diverse reaction classes, this capability would connect measured reaction kinetics to experimentally resolved structural sequences. It could reveal intermediate geometries and the structural changes associated with bond rearrangements in non-photoactive enzymes and crystalline chemical systems, on the timescales relevant to their chemistry. Existing mixing-triggered enzyme experiments and photo-triggered framework experiments provide concrete foundations for that conditional advance.

The movie analogy has important limits. Diffraction measures ensemble information, and inferred structures can depend on kinetic models, occupancy estimates and extrapolation. Even an atomic-resolution electron-density series would not automatically show proton transfer: assigning hydrogen positions and proton movement would require adequate hydrogen sensitivity and complementary evidence. The scientific gain would be stronger experimental constraints on mechanisms, with uncertainty retained wherever competing pathways explain the observations.

Conditional downstream possibilities include more informed catalyst design and better explanations of how temperature, substrate delivery or electrical conditions alter a reaction. These are reasoned possibilities, not demonstrated consequences of the proposed innovation. A structural sequence would not by itself deliver a better catalyst, establish that the same pathway operates outside the crystal, or make every chemical reaction experimentally accessible.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central missing capability is a broadly transferable combination of reaction initiation, synchronization, diffraction sampling and structural interpretation that resolves non-photoinitiated elementary chemistry on its own timescale. Reaction timing must be sufficiently well defined across the illuminated volume and across serial specimens. Nominal exposure duration or a short delivery transit time alone does not establish effective reaction-time resolution. The supplied evidence demonstrates selected implementations, but does not establish access to arbitrary elementary steps.

Substrate delivery introduces system-dependent diffusion and population problems: molecules may reach different regions of a crystal at different times, leaving several reaction states superimposed in the diffraction data. Collecting additional delays is useful only if those populations can be separated well enough to identify and order the chemistry. The xylose-isomerase study explicitly describes difficulty interpreting overlapping states from electron density alone, illustrating the gap between observing turnover-associated changes and uniquely resolving an elementary step.

Irreversible chemistry complicates repeated measurements because a specimen cannot necessarily be reset for another reaction cycle. This does not mean that every irreversible reaction physically destroys its crystal. Serial crystallography already addresses this limitation by measuring fresh specimens, but extending the approach requires reproducible reaction preparation and sufficiently complete diffraction data from comparable populations.

Further engineering questions concern synchronized electrical initiation and rapid thermal initiation across specimens. These remain targets identified by the concept; the supplied review does not establish their detailed limitations or current performance. Preparing a crystal at a selected temperature and then adding substrate must be distinguished from abruptly triggering a reaction with a temperature change. Likewise, whether lattice constraints alter motions or pathways relevant to solution or surface chemistry requires reaction-specific validation rather than a blanket assumption.

current_state.text: The July 2025 multi-temperature serial-crystallography study demonstrated substrate-triggered turnover measurements for CTX-M-14 β-lactamase at 20, 30 and 37 °C, using a 3 s delay. For xylose isomerase, the reported reaction measurements covered 20–50 °C with 60 s delays, with additional 180 s measurements at 20 and 50 °C. These are selected non-photoactive enzyme achievements. They establish temperature-dependent turnover measurements, but do not by themselves establish elementary-step resolution on arbitrary reaction timescales.

The same apparatus supported environmental-control ranges of 7–55 °C and 50 °C to above 70 °C through separate modules. Thus, the broad description of operation from below 10 °C to above 70 °C concerns apparatus capability; turnover was not demonstrated throughout that range. These experiments used substrate addition at controlled temperatures, which does not establish rapid temperature-jump initiation.

The 2024 metal–organic-framework study reported photoinduced CO dissociation and structural dynamics in PCN–224(Fe)–CO, initiated by a 400 nm femtosecond laser pulse. It obtained electron-density maps across many delays and used kinetic and structural analysis to interpret the evolving species. Its reported novelty was the extension of time-resolved serial femtosecond crystallography to a non-protein chemical crystal; the paper acknowledged earlier static chemical serial femtosecond crystallography. It therefore supplies an important photo-triggered precedent, rather than a demonstration of the proposed non-photochemical capability.

The reconciled research attributes millisecond mixing, a below-2-ms synchrotron example and a shortage of suitable reaction-triggering tools to the July 2024 ACS Catalysis review. No text or artifact from that source was retained in the supplied evidence, so these particular assertions cannot be checked here. They remain unresolved rather than disproved and should not be treated as established timing benchmarks. The separately mentioned 0.5 ms droplet flight time does not establish sub-2-ms effective reaction resolution.

The supplied review was based on complete retained article text for the two Nature studies, together with supplementary and peer-review material used for the enzyme study. Its assessment concerned the textual reports; figures and electron-density-map images were not visually inspected. The dated demonstrations are therefore supported at the level described in that review. However, the freshness record is empty, so these inputs cannot establish whether a general thermal or electrochemical elementary-step capability remained unavailable as of November 1, 2026. That gap does not invalidate the reported 2024 and 2025 achievements.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed breadth demonstration: measure three chemically unrelated non-photoactive reactions, including at least one small-molecule or heterogeneous catalytic step, with each reaction initiated without a photochemical trigger. For every case, obtain maps at enough delays, spatial resolution and effective temporal resolution to identify and order the elementary step. Three reactions would demonstrate a specified breadth of applicability, not literal universality. This is a proposed benchmark, not an established community standard.
completion_criteria.label: Ordered elementary-step maps across three unrelated reactions without photochemical triggers

completion_criteria.text: Proposed measurement requirements: pre-register the spatial-resolution target, effective timing uncertainty, temporal sampling, population-separation requirements and acceptable uncertainty in structural assignments. Demonstrate that the data distinguish the claimed sequence from plausible alternative sequences or mixtures. Repeat the measurements across independent sample preparations and make the diffraction data, timing characterization and analysis sufficiently available for independent reanalysis and reproduction. One trapped intermediate or one photo-pumped oscillation would not satisfy the proposed scope.
completion_criteria.label: Pre-registered measurements reproducibly distinguish claimed sequences from plausible alternatives

completion_criteria.text: Proposed fidelity requirements: compare orthogonal kinetics and mechanism-sensitive measurements inside and outside the lattice within pre-registered tolerances appropriate to each reaction. Matching overall rates alone would not establish an unchanged mechanism. The supplied peer-review discussion notes that crystal and solution reaction rates can differ; this is expert context motivating a fidelity check, rather than a comparative kinetic result established by that study.
completion_criteria.label: Lattice and nonlattice kinetics and mechanisms match pre-registered tolerances

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundaries: report which crystal forms, specimen sizes, trigger conditions, reaction rates and irreversible sampling requirements are compatible with the method, together with failures and unresolved assignments. If proton transfer is claimed, include evidence sufficient to support hydrogen-sensitive interpretation. Completion would mean reproducible elementary-step movies within clearly demonstrated operating conditions, with broader applicability remaining a question for further experiments.
completion_criteria.label: Report demonstrated operating conditions, failures, and unresolved structural assignments

related_concepts.text: Roster-based distinction: CRX-12, “Continuous atomic-resolution crystallography inside working devices and static extreme environments,” overlaps through measurements under applied conditions, including electrical operation. CRX-06 specifically requires identifying and ordering elementary chemical changes; continuous device diffraction alone need not provide that assignment. Conversely, a triggered reaction sequence need not involve a continuously operating device. The two entries retain separate goals.

Roster-based distinction: CRX-08, “Ab initio atomic structure of matter that exists only once,” concerns structure recovery when the target exists only once. CRX-06 can consume many fresh specimens while reconstructing a reproducible reaction sequence, so destructive or irreversible sampling is compatible with it. CRX-01, “Atomic-resolution imaging of a single non-crystalline molecule before destruction,” shares the challenge of obtaining information before specimen loss, but targets an individual non-crystalline molecule rather than a crystallographic reaction series.

Roster-based distinction: CRX-09, “Protonation state as a routine crystallographic observable,” would strengthen CRX-06 where proton positions or transfers determine the mechanism. Ordering a reaction structurally and establishing its protonation changes remain distinct achievements. CRX-04, “Atomic ensembles measured from total X-ray scattering,” shares the problem of interpreting structural populations, while its defining measurement target differs from resolving a triggered elementary-step sequence.

Roster-based distinction: CRX-11, “Diffraction-quality crystals of arbitrary macromolecules on demand,” could broaden access to suitable enzyme specimens, while CRX-10, “Laboratory sources that do facility-class coherent X-ray crystallography,” could broaden access to enabling instrumentation. Neither goal alone supplies synchronized reaction initiation or reliable elementary-step assignment. These are potential enabling relationships, not reasons to merge the entries.

The research connects this concept to an earlier historical item seeking a movie of any reaction. That item's original wording and scope were not supplied. It can therefore be retained only as a reported motivation; the present concept's identity rests on broad, validated access to elementary steps initiated without a photochemical trigger.

brief.title: Movies of atoms rearranging without a flash of light
possible: Researchers could reconstruct how atoms rearrange during a single chemical step started by mixing ingredients, heating or applying voltage. Maps of atomic positions taken at successive moments would establish which changes happen first.
They could follow reactions that light cannot start, across a wider range of chemistry. The resulting movies would connect reaction speeds with the changing structures of the reacting molecules.
why: Knowing the shapes molecules pass through during a reaction would help researchers explain how bonds rearrange. It would give them stronger experimental grounds for choosing between competing explanations of how a reaction works.

For researchers designing catalysts, substances that help reactions proceed, those structures could guide better designs. They could also help explain how temperature, ingredient delivery or electrical conditions change a reaction.

sources.who: Authors of the ACS Catalysis review
sources.showed: This review discusses tools for starting reactions and mixing-based measurements of structural changes over time.
sources.cited_for: It provides context on reaction-starting tools and mixing-based experiments.
sources.not_established: A review does not demonstrate broadly usable atomic sequences of individual chemical steps started without light.

sources.who: Eike C. Schulz, Pedram Mehrabi and collaborators
sources.showed: They added reacting ingredients to enzyme crystals held at controlled temperatures and measured structural changes. They showed that temperature changed how quickly these biological catalysts processed the ingredients.
sources.quote: Here, we show for both systems that a modification of the environmental temperature modulates the underlying structural dynamics as well as the enzyme kinetics.
sources.cited_for: Reactions started by adding ingredients can already be studied structurally at different temperatures.
sources.not_established: These enzyme measurements do not establish the ordered atomic changes of individual steps across diverse reactions.

sources.who: Jaedong Kang, Hyotcherl Ihee and collaborators
sources.showed: They used laser light to start a reaction in a crystal framework built from metal-containing units. Atomic maps revealed branching structural changes, including oscillating atoms and temporary distortions.
sources.quote: The time-resolved electron density maps derived from the TR-SFX data unveil trifurcating structural pathways: coherent oscillatory movements of Zr and Fe atoms
sources.cited_for: Atomic maps over time can reveal structural changes in chemical crystals beyond proteins.
sources.not_established: The reaction began with light, so it does not demonstrate the required capability with other triggers.

shown: Schulz, Mehrabi and collaborators have measured temperature-dependent enzyme reactions started by adding ingredients to crystals. Kang, Ihee and collaborators have mapped structural changes in a chemical crystal after a laser pulse.
missing: A broadly transferable method must resolve and order individual chemical steps started without light, at the speed each reaction actually proceeds.
Reaction timing must be consistent across crystals, and overlapping reacting populations must be separated well enough to identify their sequence.
Fresh specimens must reproducibly capture comparable reaction stages when an irreversible reaction cannot be reset.
Each reaction needs evidence that the crystal preserves the pathway relevant outside it.

milestones.label: Ordered atomic maps across three unrelated reactions without light
milestones.explanation: Three unrelated reactions must yield ordered maps of individual chemical steps without light, including a simple-molecule or surface-catalyst step. This would demonstrate breadth beyond selected enzymes.

milestones.label: Repeatable measurements distinguish competing sequences
milestones.explanation: Measurements must meet advance-set limits for detail, timing, sampling, mixed states and uncertainty, repeat across independent preparations, and permit independent reanalysis and reproduction. This would distinguish competing sequences.

milestones.label: Reaction speeds and pathways match inside and outside crystals
milestones.explanation: Independent measurements must show matching reaction speeds and pathways inside and outside crystals within advance-set tolerances. This would establish that the crystal preserves the chemistry being studied.

milestones.label: Working conditions, failures and unresolved structures are reported
milestones.explanation: Results must report usable crystals, sizes, triggers, reaction speeds, irreversible sampling needs, failures and unresolved structures, with hydrogen evidence for claimed proton movement. This would define where the movies are reliable.

uncertain: The acceptable limits for atomic detail, timing uncertainty, separating mixed states and matching chemistry remain to be defined.
How reliably can voltage or rapid heating start the same reaction at the same time across many crystals?
Several pathways may fit the same maps; atomic detail alone may not reveal proton movement, the transfer of hydrogen nuclei.

page.title: Non-photoinitiated time-resolved crystallography
page.definition: Diffraction from reacting crystals would resolve the ordered atomic changes within an elementary chemical step, a single reaction event, initiated without photochemistry. Time-dependent electron-density maps, which describe electrons around atoms, would distinguish changes within the step as well as the species before and after it.

goal.need: A crystallographic best-practice paper estimates that fewer than 0.5% of proteins are naturally photosensitive and reports a median enzyme turnover rate of 13.7 s−1. Chemical initiation opens targets inaccessible to direct photoactivation, with many turnovers occurring on millisecond-to-second timescales. Resolving accumulated intermediates still leaves the faster atomic changes between them to be established.

statements.quote: The goal is to achieve (near-)atomic resolution determination of static structures or ultrafast structural dynamics (millisecond to femtosecond timescale) in these specimens.
statements.context: The science programme includes enzyme–substrate mixing experiments and applications to non-biological samples.

statements.body: SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory, Structural Dynamics of Biomolecules Resource
statements.quote: to develop more generalized time-resolved approaches applicable to non-photoactive systems
statements.context: The programme includes photocages and laser heating alongside separately described mix-and-inject crystallography.

completion.title: Atomic changes within a non-photoinitiated elementary reaction step are resolved in time.
completion.criterion: For one reaction initiated without photochemistry, time-ordered electron-density maps distinguish atomic changes within one chemically identified elementary step. Reaction-initiation spread, probe duration and timing uncertainty are short enough to resolve those changes. Population analysis distinguishes their order from unresolved mixtures of the states before and after the step, and complementary chemical measurements support the assignment. Structures of successive long-lived intermediates alone do not meet this test.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; a reaction-specific synthesis of published crystallographic requirements, without a numerical breadth requirement.
completion.basis: Searched IUCr best-practice papers, the ACS Catalysis review, European XFEL and LCLS programmes, and recent enzyme papers for a non-photoinitiated elementary-step benchmark; found no completion test or universal numerical acceptance limits. This test covers one step in one reaction. The 2026 isopenicillin N synthase paper distinguishes observed intermediates from chemical steps it infers.

milestones.title: A reaction proceeds in a crystal that retains interpretable diffraction.
milestones.criterion: The reaction occurs without initiation or progress preventing structural measurement. Published on 16 July 2025, substrate-triggered measurements of two enzymes, CTX-M-14 β-lactamase and xylose isomerase, used 3 s and 60 s delays, respectively, at controlled temperatures. For synthetic crystals, the study published on 25 March 2024 obtained electron-density maps of one PCN–224(Fe)–CO framework across 33 delays after a 400 nm pulse. That experiment establishes this prerequisite through photochemical initiation.
milestones.set_by: Field feasibility criteria summarized by Mark A. Wilson, section 3 of his structural-enzymology review; originally stated for enzyme crystals.
milestones.threshold_quote: the reaction must occur in the crystal 2) the crystal must not be damaged by reaction initiation or progress

milestones.title: A non-photoinitiated reaction yields an intermediate before its end state.
milestones.criterion: An early-delay structure contains an intermediate rather than only final-state species. The guideline's 10–20 ms example is not a universal cutoff. Published on 31 May 2018, the BlaC β-lactamase/ceftriaxone experiment used two crystal forms; substrate complexes appeared at 30 ms and a covalent intermediate dominated at 500 ms.
milestones.set_by: Schulz, Yorke, Pearson and Mehrabi, Best practices for time-resolved serial synchrotron crystallography, section 6.2; written for protein crystals.
milestones.threshold_quote: whether the reaction is slow enough to be resolved by TR-SSX, i.e. whether the end state has already been reached or not.

milestones.title: A non-photoinitiated reaction yields intermediate structures and a compatible kinetic mechanism.
milestones.criterion: Intermediate structures and their changing populations admit a chemically compatible kinetic mechanism. Compatibility does not establish uniqueness. In the BlaC/ceftriaxone study, simulations included substrate diffusion and product inhibition; the authors explicitly allowed other mechanisms to explain the observations.
milestones.set_by: Time-resolved crystallographic analysis convention summarized by Marius Schmidt in Biological function investigated by time-resolved structure determination; described for biomolecular reactions.
milestones.threshold_quote: the structures of the intermediates as well as a compatible kinetic mechanism

milestones.title: A non-photoinitiated reaction has compatible diffraction and spectroscopic intermediate assignments.
milestones.criterion: Diffraction-derived intermediates have chemical-state assignments compatible with independent spectroscopy. Published on 9 October 2026, one isopenicillin N synthase system with a deuterium-labelled peptide substrate was triggered by oxygen. Seven delays were 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8 and 10 s; XFEL results were repeated at least twice. X-ray emission spectroscopy supported iron-state assignments consistent with earlier solution Mössbauer studies. Peroxide deprotonation and ferryl formation were inferred rather than directly imaged.
milestones.set_by: Orthogonal chemical-state corroboration applied by Rabe and colleagues, Discussion; the quoted application is specific to isopenicillin N synthase. Complementary spectroscopy is also described in crystallographic best-practice guidance.
milestones.threshold_quote: The combined XES spectral trends and structural results are consistent with prior solution-phase Mössbauer studies of IPNS

not_found: No external completion benchmark was found for non-photoinitiated imaging within an elementary chemical step.
No common numerical acceptance limits were found for spatial resolution, initiation spread, state occupancy or agreement with solution chemistry.
Searches did not establish a thermal, electrical or synthetic-crystal demonstration satisfying the completion criterion.
The IUPAC Gold Book elementary-reaction entry and its PDF returned access errors.

results.finding: Two substrate-triggered enzyme systems yielded structural measurements at delays of 3 s and 60 s.
results.detail: CTX-M-14 and xylose isomerase crystals were measured at controlled temperatures after substrate addition.
results.quote:
To assess thermal effects on catalysis, we equilibrated the crystals at a given temperature and triggered their reaction by adding the substrate solution
via
the LAMA method
43
and monitored turnover at a constant time-delay of 3 s (CTX-M-14) and 60 s (XI) after reaction initiation, respectively

results.finding: One CTX-M-14 reaction showed an acyl-enzyme intermediate in the 3 s structure.
results.detail: At 30 °C, refinement indicated a mixture dominated by the intermediate and hydrolysed product; at 37 °C the structure was predominantly product-bound.
results.quote: Occupancy refinement indicated a mixture corresponding predominantly to the acyl-enzyme-intermediate and a complex with the hydrolysed piperacillin product.

results.finding: One CTX-M-14 reaction showed changing catalytic-state populations at a 3 s delay.
results.detail: The observed states are consistent with substrate binding, acylation and hydrolysis, but the paper does not fit a kinetic mechanism to time-dependent intermediate populations. The comparison primarily varies temperature.
results.quote:
Since different catalytic sub-states of CTX-M-14 can clearly be distinguished at different temperatures (unbound state, acyl-enzyme intermediate, hydrolysed piperacillin product Fig.
3
a–c), these data also show that turnover kinetics of mesophilic enzymes can be modulated by temperature variation in our control box.

results.finding: One PCN–224(Fe)–CO framework yielded electron-density maps across 33 delays during CO dissociation.
results.detail: A 400 nm laser pulse initiated the reaction; fresh crystals were exposed for measurements.
results.quote: By indexing the diffraction patterns and extracting the scattering amplitudes, we obtained ED maps for all time delays.

results.finding: One iridium-complex single crystal reacted with H₂ and retained interpretable diffraction at 1.2 Å resolution.
results.detail: The reaction was measured in situ under hydrogen. Diffraction quality deteriorated after reaction, and the hydrides could not be located; their presence was confirmed by NMR.
results.quote:
Addition of H 2 (2 bar) to the same single crystal used for the
structural analysis of complex 6 at 273 K led to the formation
of complex 7, for which a satisfactory structural solution could
be determined

results.finding: Copper amine oxidase microcrystals, number not reported: a catalytic intermediate was captured at 22 ms.
results.detail: Substrate mixing initiated the reaction under anaerobic conditions. The earlier substrate Schiff-base intermediate was not captured, possibly because substrate diffusion was slow.
results.quote:
The slower decay of
TPQpsb compared to its formation, even at Δtm = 22 ms, is likely the
reason for its capture as a metastable intermediate16,21.

results.finding: One synthetic porous-network crystal yielded 34% hemiaminal after 10 minutes.
results.detail: Acetaldehyde reacted with embedded amine at 215 K; the crystal was cooled to 90 K for diffraction. Warming to 270 K for 30 minutes produced the final imine.
results.quote:
The X-ray crystal structure after 10 min at 215 K 
revealed the unstable hemiaminal intermediate along with 
unreacted amine.

results.finding: BlaC–ceftriaxone in 2 crystal forms: the acyl intermediate peaked at 500 ms, consistent with a simulated kinetic mechanism.
results.detail: Mixing initiated the reaction. Simulations incorporated substrate diffusion and assumed product inhibition. Four post-mixing time points did not independently determine the kinetic parameters; alternative mechanisms could explain the observations.
results.quote: After initial formation of the ES complex represented by a non-covalently bound full-length CEF, the intermediate E-CFO* has its peak concentration at 500 ms.

results.finding: Copper amine oxidase microcrystals: 12 structures at 9 time points; TPQamr occupancy reached 0% at 1000 ms.
results.detail: Substrate mixing initiated the reaction. Intermediate populations supported a reaction sequence incorporating substrate diffusion and a proposed diffusion-controlled ligand exchange. The first predicted intermediate was not captured, and product and substrate could not be distinguished directly by their electron densities.
results.quote:
Occupancy of
TPQamr relative to TPQ sq, calculated after structural re ﬁnement,
decreased gradually with the increase in Δtm and reached 0% at
1000 ms (Fig. 3c).

results.finding: Rhodium complex crystals (sample count not stated): a cyclooctane intermediate was structurally resolved after 40 minutes of D2 exposure.
results.detail: NMR and quenching experiments tracked changing species populations; a sequential kinetic model fit the reaction course. The detailed mechanism was proposed, with alternative rate-determining steps possible. Diffraction and kinetic measurements used different-sized samples.
results.quote:
By optimizing the time of D2 addition a structural so-
lution for dx-[1-COA][BArF4] could be obtained after 40 minu-
tes using single-crystal X-ray diffraction.

results.finding: One IPNS enzyme-crystal system showed diffraction intermediates with spectroscopically compatible iron states across seven delays.
results.detail: Oxygen initiated the reaction in crystals containing deuterium-labelled substrate; XFEL results were repeated at least twice. X-ray emission spectroscopy and structural assignments were consistent with earlier solution Mössbauer studies. Peroxide deprotonation and ferryl formation were not directly visualized.
results.quote:
combined XES spectral trends and structural results are consistent with 
prior solution-phase Mössbauer studies of IPNS, which independently 
identified Fe(III)-superoxo and Fe(IV)=O intermediates 4.

results.finding: One synthetic porous-network crystal contained 34% hemiaminal; IR spectroscopy agreed with the X-ray results.
results.detail: Acetaldehyde reacted with embedded amine at low temperature. Single-crystal microscopic IR measurements under the same conditions supported the diffraction assignments.
results.quote:
The chemical reactions in the pore were
monitored by single crystal microscopic IR spectroscopy
under the same conditions.  The temperature dependent
measurement showed excellent agreement with the X-ray
results.
